title: DevOps
intro: A small but precise domain: how Pega applications move through a CI/CD pipeline with Deployment Manager, and which automated tests (unit tests, test cases, assertions, coverage) give confidence to deploy. Questions usually test pipeline stage names, assertion types and coverage roles.

objectives.objective: Explain Pega’s process of continuous development, integration, delivery, and deployment (CI/CD)
summary: DevOps combines people, process and technology so that development, QA and operations work as one flow, covering development, testing and post-go-live support. **Continuous integration** means frequent check-ins with automated builds and tests: changes become ready to share, are integrated, and are published to a development repository. **Continuous delivery** adds automated regression and staging, then moves through ready to accept (acceptance criteria), ready to deploy (performance, scale and compatibility), and deployment (validate in pre-production, deploy to production, run post-deployment tests, roll back if needed). A typical setup pairs a Pega repository with an automation server such as Jenkins.

**Deployment Manager** is Pega's own CI/CD pipeline tool: it merges branches, packages and promotes applications. It is accessed in Admin Studio and integrates with App Studio, where Settings > Versions lets you publish to higher environments. Third-party tools such as Jenkins and Azure DevOps can also be used. Deployment Manager blocks a production deployment if the Security Checklist has not been completed.

CI best practices: test early and often (run Pega unit tests and critical integration tests before packaging and stop the pipeline on failure), automate merges and builds, keep the product rule (Rule-Admin-Product) current, and publish archives to a repository for version history. CD best practices: use test environments (for example Docker) for UAT and exploratory testing, run regression through UI and service layers, target specific ruleset versions for production, roll back the latest import on failure, and annotate a package as ready to deploy before manual or automatic deployment.
keyFacts: CI stages: ready to share, integrate changes, publish to development repository.
CD stages: ready to accept (acceptance criteria), ready to deploy (performance, scale, compatibility), deploy.
Deploy includes pre-production validation, production deployment, post-deployment tests and rollback.
Deployment Manager = Pega's CI/CD tool for branch merge, packaging and promotion; opened in Admin Studio.
From App Studio, Settings > Versions publishes to higher environments through Deployment Manager.
Deployment Manager blocks production deployment when the Security Checklist is incomplete.
Stop the pipeline when unit or critical integration tests fail.
Keep Rule-Admin-Product up to date and publish archives to a repository.
On a failed production import, roll back the latest import.
Testing cycles: Pega unit, regression, performance, load.

rows: Is my change ready for others (CI)?
Does it merge and build cleanly with everyone else's work?
Does it meet performance, scale and compatibility needs?
Validate in pre-production, deploy, post-deploy test, roll back if needed

examTraps: Performance, scale and compatibility belong to ready to deploy, not ready to accept.
Deployment Manager lives in Admin Studio, not Dev Studio.
Skipping tests to speed up the pipeline contradicts CI best practice.
A blocked production deployment can come from an incomplete Security Checklist even when tests pass.

objectives.objective: Describe the tests required for successful deployment: unit tests, test cases, and assertions
summary: The smallest testable unit is an individual rule, so unit tests isolate where an error comes from (for example whether the decision tree or the data page is wrong). Rule resolution applies during tests. A unit test run can be converted into a reusable **test case** with assertions: Property (for example `pxUrgencyWork` equals 10), Decision result, Expected run time (for example within 3 seconds) and Page (for example a list data page has no errors). Test cases can be grouped into test suites and should run at least on every merge and check-in.

Automate first where results are predictable, tests run often, manual effort on complex logic is high, or the rule is widely used. Low-priority candidates are rules that change frequently, are easy to test manually, are too complex, or depend on database persistence. Good tests cover positive and negative paths and are maintainable (clear names, comments, modular test data).

Test case details: the Disable checkbox excludes a test from suites and REST runs so it can only be run manually; the Setup & Cleanup tab prepares and removes data with data transforms, activities and clipboard pages; the label becomes the immutable identifier. Flows and case types are recorded with Actions > Record test case; captured inputs go into a data transform, and the `pxCapturePropertyIgnore` data transform excludes properties from capture. Since 8.5, a process containing the Create stage of a new case type cannot be recorded. Strategy tests use componentName and pzRandomSeed parameters.
keyFacts: Unit = individual rule; rule resolution still applies in tests.
Assertion types: Property, Decision result, Expected run time, Page.
Group test cases into test suites; run at least on every merge and check-in.
High automation priority: predictable, frequently run, complex manual effort, widely used.
Low automation priority: frequently changing, easy manually, too complex, database persistence.
Disabled test cases are excluded from suites and REST runs; manual run only.
Setup & Cleanup tab handles test data with data transforms, activities and clipboard pages.
Recorded flow inputs are stored in a data transform; exclude properties with pxCapturePropertyIgnore.
A test case label becomes its identifier, which cannot be changed.

rows: A decision rule returns the expected result
A data page has no errors

examTraps: A rule that changes frequently is a poor automation candidate, even if it is important.
Disabled does not mean deleted; the test can still be run manually.
Excluding a volatile property from a recording uses pxCapturePropertyIgnore, not the cleanup tab.

objectives.objective: Describe the tests required for successful deployment: the test pyramid and test coverage
summary: The **test pyramid** puts unit tests at the base because they are cheap, fast and should be the most numerous; end-to-end tests sit at the top because they are expensive and should be few.

The **test coverage** tool reports which rules were exercised; an uncovered rule is one that was not tested. User-level reports cover one user's session and keep a coverage history. Application-level reports combine data from multiple users, appear in the Application Quality Dashboard, and can be merged. Running test suites requires SysAdm4; only operators with SysAdm4 or User4 contribute coverage data; starting application-level coverage needs the `pzStartOrStopMasterAppRuleCoverage` privilege. Coverage and pass rate also feed branch quality metrics.
keyFacts: Pyramid: many unit tests at the base, few end-to-end tests at the top.
Uncovered rule = a rule not executed by any test.
User-level coverage: single user, coverage history.
Application-level coverage: multiple users, Application Quality Dashboard, reports can be merged.
SysAdm4 is required to run test suites.
Only SysAdm4 or User4 operators contribute coverage data.
Starting application-level coverage requires pzStartOrStopMasterAppRuleCoverage.

rows: Application Quality Dashboard; reports can be merged

examTraps: An uncovered rule is untested, not a rule whose test failed.
Application-level coverage cannot be started by any operator; it needs a specific privilege.
An inverted pyramid (mostly end-to-end tests) is slow and costly.

questions.stem: Release 3.2 of a claims application has passed its acceptance criteria. Before production, operations must confirm that it performs under expected load, scales and is compatible with the target environment. Which pipeline checkpoint is this?
options: Ready to share
Integrate changes
Ready to accept
Ready to deploy
questions.explanation: In continuous delivery, "ready to deploy" covers performance, scale and compatibility checks before production. "Ready to accept" is the earlier checkpoint where acceptance criteria are verified, and this release has already passed it. "Ready to share" and "integrate changes" are continuous integration steps that publish developer changes to the development repository.

questions.stem: Every automated test passes and the package is marked ready to deploy, but Deployment Manager blocks the deployment to production. Which cause is most likely?
options: The Security Checklist for the application has not been completed.
The pipeline does not use Jenkins as its automation server.
The application's product rule includes ruleset versions that are locked.
The release was not started from App Studio Settings > Versions.
questions.explanation: Deployment Manager blocks a production deployment until the Security Checklist is completed and IT security approves it. Jenkins is an optional third-party tool, and Deployment Manager is Pega's own CI/CD tool. Locking ruleset versions is a recommended practice and does not block deployment. Settings > Versions is one way to publish from App Studio, not a requirement for production.

questions.stem: A team wants its continuous integration process to catch problems earlier. Which two practices follow Pega CI guidance? (Choose Two)
options: Run Pega unit tests and critical integration tests before packaging, and stop the pipeline on a failure.
Keep the product rule (Rule-Admin-Product) up to date.
Run unit tests after packaging so the archive is built sooner.
Keep archives out of the repository so that only the latest build exists.
questions.explanation: Pega CI guidance is to test early and often: run Pega unit tests and critical integration tests before packaging, and stop the pipeline when one fails. Teams should also automate merges and builds, keep the product rule up to date, and publish archives to a repository to keep version history. Running tests after packaging delays feedback, which is the wrong order. Keeping archives out of the repository loses the version history that the repository exists to keep.

questions.stem: An operations lead is reviewing the team's continuous delivery practices. Which two practices match Pega CD guidance? (Choose Two)
options: Roll back the latest import when a deployment fails.
Use test environments such as Docker for UAT and exploratory testing.
Run regression tests only through the UI layer.
Allow only manual deployment to production because automatic deployment is not supported.
questions.explanation: Pega CD guidance includes rolling back the latest import when a deployment fails, and using test environments such as Docker for UAT and exploratory testing. Regression testing should run through both the UI layer and the service layer, not the UI alone. Deployment to production can be manual or automatic, so automatic deployment is supported.

questions.stem: A system architect working in App Studio wants to promote the current application version to higher environments through the company's Deployment Manager pipeline. Where does she start?
options: Settings > Versions
Library > Reuse Library
Users > User management
The Case Types explorer
questions.explanation: Deployment Manager is accessed in Admin Studio. When it is integrated with App Studio, a developer publishes to higher environments from Settings > Versions. The Reuse Library is a catalog of reusable assets. User management handles personas and access. The Case Types explorer is for designing cases. None of these three starts a pipeline.

questions.stem: A QA lead has budget to automate unit tests for one more rule. Which candidate is the lowest priority for automation?
options: A widely used Decision table with predictable results
A pricing rule whose logic changes nearly every sprint
A complex calculation that runs many times a day
A When rule called by dozens of flows
questions.explanation: Rules whose logic changes often are a low priority for automation because the tests need constant upkeep. Other low-priority candidates are rules that are easy to test by hand, rules too complex to test reliably, and database persistence. High-priority candidates have predictable results, run often, are widely used, or save manual effort on complex logic. The Decision table, the complex calculation and the widely called When rule all fit that profile.

questions.stem: A tester converts a unit test run into a test case. It must confirm that the case urgency `pxUrgencyWork` equals 10 and that the rule finishes within 3 seconds. Which two assertion types should be added? (Choose Two)
options: Property assertion
Expected run time assertion
Decision result assertion
Page assertion
questions.explanation: A Property assertion checks a specific property value, such as pxUrgencyWork = 10. An Expected run time assertion checks that the rule finishes within a limit, such as 3 seconds. A Decision result assertion checks the result returned by a decision rule, not the value of a case property. A Page assertion checks a page as a whole, for example that D_CoursesList has no errors.

questions.stem: A developer selects the Disable checkbox on a test case that has become unreliable. What is the effect?
options: The test case is removed from suites and REST runs, but can still be run manually.
The test case still runs in suites, but its failures are ignored.
The test case cannot be run in any way until it is enabled again.
The test case is deleted at the next Branch merge.
questions.explanation: A disabled test case is left out of test suites and REST API runs, but a developer can still run it manually. It does not stay in suites with its failures ignored. Manual runs remain possible, so it is not completely blocked. Disabling a test case does not delete it.

questions.stem: A QA analyst records test cases for the Onboarding flow. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose Two)
options: The captured inputs are stored in a Data Transform.
Properties listed in the pxCapturePropertyIgnore Data Transform are not captured.
From version 8.5, a new Case Type's process that includes the Create stage can be recorded.
A test case identifier can be renamed later by editing its Label.
questions.explanation: Recording a test case with Actions > Record test case stores the captured inputs in a Data Transform. Properties such as changing timestamps can be excluded through the pxCapturePropertyIgnore Data Transform. Since 8.5, a process that includes the Create stage for new Case Types cannot be recorded, which is the reverse of the statement offered. The Label sets the identifier when the test case is created, and the identifier cannot be changed afterward.

questions.stem: A team has 400 end-to-end UI tests and 20 unit tests. Builds take hours, and failures are hard to trace. What does the test pyramid recommend?
options: Shift toward many unit tests at the base and keep only a few end-to-end tests at the top.
Add more end-to-end tests, because they cover the most functionality for each test.
Keep the same balance but run the end-to-end tests less often.
Replace the unit tests with load tests, which find failures faster.
questions.explanation: The test pyramid puts cheap, fast and numerous unit tests at the base and a few expensive end-to-end tests at the top. This team's pyramid is upside down. Unit tests isolate errors at the level of a single rule, so failures are easier to trace. Adding end-to-end tests makes the imbalance worse. Running them less often does not fix how hard failures are to trace. Load testing is a different testing cycle, not a replacement for unit tests.

questions.stem: A quality manager wants one view of rule coverage across testing done by six developers. Which two statements are correct? (Choose Two)
options: Application-level coverage combines data from several users and is shown in the Application Quality Dashboard.
Starting application-level coverage requires the pzStartOrStopMasterAppRuleCoverage privilege.
User-level coverage reports can be merged to combine results from several users.
Any operator, including one with WorkMgr4, contributes coverage data while testing.
questions.explanation: Application-level coverage collects data from several users, is viewed in the Application Quality Dashboard, and needs the pzStartOrStopMasterAppRuleCoverage privilege to start. User-level reports cover one user and show that user's coverage history. Merging reports is a feature of application-level coverage. Only operators with SysAdm4 or User4 contribute coverage data, so WorkMgr4 does not.

questions.stem: A QA analyst has the User4 role. She can contribute coverage data, but cannot run the team's test suites. What explains this?
options: Running test suites requires the SysAdm4 role.
Test suites can run only from a Deployment Manager pipeline.
User4 operators cannot run any unit tests.
The suites contain test cases marked as uncovered rules.
questions.explanation: Running test suites requires SysAdm4. User4 can contribute coverage data, which matches what the analyst sees. Test suites are not limited to Deployment Manager pipelines. Nothing in the role prevents unit testing in general. An uncovered rule is one that no test exercised. The term describes coverage results, not test cases, and it does not affect who can run a suite.
